findings.title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op due to the monkeypatch, so the test is still racy
findings.body: At the top of test_basic, `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` patches time.sleep to do nothing. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` (with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") therefore sleeps for zero time and provides no synchronization at all. The test still depends on the flusher thread noticing `current_drift.value = 9000` and flushing the segment before `step.join()` sets the stopped flag; if join wins the race, no message is produced and `(msg,) = messages` fails. This makes the test flaky — the added sleep gives a false impression that the race was fixed. Use a real wait (e.g., poll `messages` with a deadline using an unpatched sleep reference captured before monkeypatching) instead.

findings.title: Restarting a hung flusher in thread mode leaves the old thread running, producing duplicate segments for the same shards
findings.body: When `produce_to_pipe` is set, flusher workers are `threading.Thread`s. In `_ensure_processes_alive`, if such a worker is judged hung (healthy_since stale), the restart path calls `process.kill()` only when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, so for threads nothing stops the old worker, and then `_create_process_for_shards` unconditionally starts a new thread for the same shards and overwrites `self.processes[process_index]`. The hung-but-alive thread and the replacement thread then concurrently call `buffer.flush_segments()` / `done_flush_segments()` for the same shards and both write to the same `process_backpressure_since`/`process_healthy_since` values, which can produce the same segment twice to the output and corrupts the health/backpressure bookkeeping. Either guard against restarting un-killable hung threads or document/handle the duplicate-flush window explicitly.

findings.title: Redis memory check double-counts clusters shared by multiple per-process buffers, skewing the used/available ratio
findings.body: Shards are assigned to processes round-robin (`process_index = i % num_processes`), so when `max_processes > 1` each per-process `SpansBuffer` typically holds shards that map to the same Redis cluster as other buffers. `submit()` now aggregates memory by calling `buffer.get_memory_info()` on every buffer and summing the results; a cluster's used/available memory is therefore counted once per covering buffer instead of once as before (previously a single buffer covered all assigned shards and could report each cluster once). If clusters are not counted a uniform number of times (e.g., cluster shard counts not divisible by the process count), the computed `used / available` ratio is skewed and `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` hard backpressure will trigger too early or too late. It also multiplies the number of Redis INFO calls made on the consumer's submit path by the number of flusher processes.

findings.title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code and would leak a duplicate process if used
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shard` is never called anywhere. Worse, if it ever were used, it calls `_create_process_for_shards` without killing the existing process for that shard's group and without incrementing `process_restarts`, leaving two live processes flushing the same shards (duplicate segments produced, conflicting health values). It should be removed or fixed to go through the same kill-and-track path as `_ensure_processes_alive`.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shards' vs 'shard'
findings.body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer uses `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` while the sibling metrics `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`. The mismatched tag key splits the time series and makes dashboards/queries grouping by `shard` miss the wait_produce data. Pick one key and use it consistently.
